Artificial intelligence (AI) now writes test items, scores essays, predicts
item difficulty and drafts analysis code. If you were trained in item
response theory (IRT), classical test theory and validity theory, you
already have the tools to judge these systems. What is usually missing is the
vocabulary, a sense of how the methods work, and practice checking them.

The AI Hub is for that reader: a psychometrician, graduate student or
testing-program analyst who knows IRT and some R, but has not trained a
machine learning model or called a large language model (LLM). Every topic
starts from a job you already do and puts the AI method beside the
classical one.

## What changes and what does not {#what-changes}

AI changes **how** some parts of a test are produced: items can be drafted
in minutes, constructed responses can be scored as they arrive, and item
properties can be estimated before a field test. It does not change **what**
a test has to show. The scores still need evidence that they mean what we
say they mean, for the people we use them with. The *Standards for
Educational and Psychological Testing* apply to an AI-scored test just as
they apply to any other.

That is why every AI feature in mirtverse sits behind a psychometric check:
generated items are verified and calibrated, machine scores must agree with
human scores overall and within groups, and anything uncertain goes back to
a person.

## A learning path {#learning-path}

Work through the steps in order, or jump to the job you face now. Each step
names the question it answers, what to read and what to try in R.

| Step | The question | Read | Try in R |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Vocabulary | What do machine learning words mean in measurement terms? | [Translation table](ai-translation.html); the AI section of the [glossary](glossary.html#ai) | — |
| 2. ML through an IRT lens | How do prediction models differ from measurement models? | Book: [Machine learning through an IRT lens](../book/ml-lens.html) | — |
| 3. LLMs in your workflow | How do I use a language model safely for analysis and writing? | [Scripts from plain language](mv-ask-guide.html); book: [Large language models as a colleague](../book/llms.html) | `mv_ask()`, `mv_llm_replay()` |
| 4. Automated scoring | Can a machine score constructed responses as well as raters? | [Reading list: automated scoring](ai-reading.html#automated-scoring) | `score_open()`; [Lab 6](teaching-labs.html) |
| 5. Item text and difficulty | What does the wording of an item tell us before anyone answers it? | [Reading list: item text](ai-reading.html#item-text) | the `itemtext` data; modelling tools coming soon |
| 6. Automatic item generation | How do I generate items and know which ones to keep? | [Assessment pipeline](assessment-pipeline.html); [reading list: AIG](ai-reading.html#aig) | `generate_items()`, `verify_items()` |
| 7. Validity and fairness | What evidence does an AI component need before it is used? | [Reading list: validity](ai-reading.html#validity) | `dif()`; audit tools coming soon |

## What you can do with AI in mirtverse today {#today}

These functions use a language model through the
[ellmer](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org) package. Set one up once with
`mv_ask_setup()`: Claude or OpenAI with your own API key, or a local model
through Ollama if your data must stay on your computer.

To try them with no key and no internet connection, turn on replay mode
first. Every request is then answered from a file of recorded responses, so
the same call always gives the same answer:

```{r}
library(mirtverse)
mv_llm_replay()      # answer from the example recordings
mv_llm_recordings()  # which requests they cover
```

The example recordings answer the calls in
`system.file("replay", "examples.R", package = "mirtverse")`, which include
the three examples below. Their responses were written by hand to show what
a model returns, with a few deliberate mistakes for mirtverse's checks to
catch. To capture your own session with a live model and replay it in
class, use `mv_llm_record()`.

### Write analysis code from a plain-language request

```{r}
mv_ask("Fit a graded response model to these attitude items, check the fit and explain the results.",
       data = Science, ask = FALSE)
```

`mv_ask()` turns the request into a plan, fills tested code templates and
shows you the script before anything runs. Without a provider it falls back
to an offline keyword parser. The [guide](mv-ask-guide.html) explains what
is sent to the model and how to keep column names private.

### Generate and verify items

```{r}
p <- mv_pipeline("Grade 6 numeracy")
p <- set_blueprint(p, blueprint)     # content areas x cognitive levels
p <- generate_items(p, n = 40)       # drafts with keys and rationales
p <- verify_items(p)                 # a second model answers each item blind
flags(p)                             # wrong keys, weak distractors, duplicates
```

A second, independent model call answers each multiple-choice item without
seeing the key; disagreements are flagged before any person reviews the
items. `review_packet(p, ai_screen = TRUE)` then prepares the human review.

### Score open-ended responses, and check the scores

```{r}
q <- score_open(q, responses, scorer = "llm")   # or a trained model
q$agreement                                     # machine-human agreement
flags(q)                                        # agreement and fairness gates
```

The full example in `examples.R` scores 40 answers from the `essays` data
against a four-point rubric.

Machine scores pass the same gates whether they come from a language model
or from a model you trained yourself: quadratic weighted kappa against human
scores, standardized mean differences overall and within groups, and
low-confidence responses routed back to human raters.

## How the AI Hub teaches {#principles}

- **Familiar job first.** Each topic opens with a task you already do and
  shows the AI method next to the classical one, on the same data.
- **Evidence before adoption.** Every AI output passes a psychometric check
  before it counts.
- **Offline by default.** Labs and book examples run without an API key or
  an internet connection, using recorded model outputs (`mv_llm_replay()`),
  so a classroom never depends on a provider being up. Live models are an
  optional extra.
- **Known answers.** As in the teaching labs, the AI datasets are simulated
  with planted problems, and `lab_truth()` reveals them. `itemtext` has 192
  numeracy items from 12 item families with field-test difficulties;
  `essays` has 1,600 short science explanations scored by raters, written
  so that fluent writers' answers are longer at the same score.

## For instructors {#instructors}

[Lab 6](teaching-labs.html), on scoring open-ended responses, already
compares an automated engine with human raters and fits well at the end of
an IRT course. The [online book](../book/index.html) has a part on AI in
measurement whose chapters work offline, so they can be assigned as
readings. More AI labs, chapters and an optional AI module for the [course
map](course-map.html) are being written; they will be listed on this page
and in the AI Hub menu as they are released.

## Read more {#read-more}

The [reading list](ai-reading.html) collects the books, papers and

worth reading. Start with the overviews at the top.
